**John Powers Severin**[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-2) ([/ˈ s ɛ v ər ɪ n/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); December 26, 1921– February 12, 2012)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-4) was an American [comics artist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comics_artist "Comics artist") noted for his distinctive work with [EC Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EC_Comics "EC Comics"), primarily on the [war comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_comics "War comics")_[Two-Fisted Tales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-Fisted\_Tales "Two-Fisted Tales")_ and _[Frontline Combat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frontline\_Combat "Frontline Combat")_; for [Marvel Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvel_Comics "Marvel Comics"), especially its war and [Western comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_comics "Western comics"); and for his 45-year stint with the [satiric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satire "Satire") magazine _[Cracked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cracked\_(magazine) "Cracked (magazine)")_. He was one of the founding cartoonists of _[Mad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mad\_(magazine) "Mad (magazine)")_ in 1952.

Severin was inducted into the [Will Eisner Award Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Eisner_Award_winners#The_Will_Eisner_Award_Hall_of_Fame "List of Eisner Award winners") in 2003.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Severin&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

John Severin was born in [Jersey City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jersey_City,_New_Jersey "Jersey City, New Jersey"), New Jersey, of Norwegian and Irish descent. He was a teenager in [Bay Ridge, Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_Ridge,_Brooklyn "Bay Ridge, Brooklyn"), New York City, when he began drawing professionally. While attending high school, he contributed cartoons to _[The Hobo News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Hobo\_News "The Hobo News")_, receiving payment of one dollar per cartoon. Severin recalled in 1999:

> I was sometimes selling 19 or 20 of them a week. Not every week, naturally. But I didn't have to get a regular job to carry me through high school. It was almost every week—not every week—but almost every week. I didn't have to get a job. I hated to work, I'll tell you. I didn't have to get a job then, because I was in high school.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-5)

He attended the [High School of Music & Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_High_School_of_Music_&_Art "The High School of Music & Art") in New York City, together with future [EC Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EC_Comics "EC Comics") and _[Mad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mad\_(magazine) "Mad (magazine)")_ artists [Harvey Kurtzman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_Kurtzman "Harvey Kurtzman"), [Will Elder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Will_Elder "Will Elder"), [Al Jaffee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jaffee "Al Jaffee") and [Al Feldstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Feldstein "Al Feldstein").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-lam-6) After graduating from the school in 1940, he worked as an apprentice machinist and then enlisted in the [Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army "United States Army"), serving in the [Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_War "Pacific War") during World War II.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-7)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Severin&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### Early work: 1947–51

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Severin&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Early work: 1947–51")]

In a 1980 interview, Severin recalled his start as a professional artist:

> I had decided to exhibit some paintings of mine in a High School of Music and Art exhibition for the alumni. Charlie Stern was in charge of it, so I went to see him at his studio. He was the "Charles" of the Charles William Harvey Studio, the other two being William Elder and Harvey Kurtzman. They asked me if I'd like to rent space with them there. I did, and started working with them. When Charlie left ... I became the third man, but they didn't want to change it to John William Harvey Studio, so they left the name ... Harvey was doing comics, Willie and Charlie were doing advertising stuff, and I just joined in ... [I did] design work, logos for toy boxes, logos for candy boxes, cards to be included in the candy boxes.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-squa36-8)

Inspired by the quick money Kurtzman would make in between advertising assignments with one-page "Hey Look!" gags for editor [Stan Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Lee "Stan Lee") at [Timely Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timely_Comics "Timely Comics"), Severin worked up comics samples inked by Elder. In late 1947, he recalled, the writer-artist-editor team of [Joe Simon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Simon "Joe Simon") and [Jack Kirby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Kirby "Jack Kirby") at [Crestwood Publications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crestwood_Publications "Crestwood Publications") "gave us our first job."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-squa36-8)

Since it was not standard practice to credit comics creators during this era, a comprehensive list of his early work is difficult to compile. Author and historian Jim Vadeboncoeur Jr., based on Severin's description of "a crime story about a boy and a girl who killed somebody ... I think it was their stepfather. They lived on a farm, or out in the suburbs," believes that first Severin/Elder story was the eight-page "The Clue of the Horoscope" in _Headline Comics_ #32 ([cover-dated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cover-date "Cover-date") Nov. 1948), from the Crestwood-affiliated [Prize Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prize_Comics "Prize Comics").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-squa36-8) The standard reference [Grand Comics Database](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Comics_Database "Grand Comics Database") has no credits for that story,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-9) and lists Severin's first confirmed work in comics as two stories published the same month: the ten-page [Boy Commandos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boy_Commandos "Boy Commandos") adventure "The Triumph of William Tell" in [DC Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DC_Comics "DC Comics")' _Boy Commandos_ #30; and the eight-page [Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_comics "Western comics") story "Grinning Hole in the Wall" in Prize Comics' _Prize Comics Western_ vol. 7, #5 (each Dec. 1948), both of which he [penciled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penciler "Penciler") and the latter of which he also [inked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inker "Inker").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-gcd-10)

Through 1955, Severin drew a large number of stories for the latter title and other Western series from Prize, and as penciler, he co-created with an unknown writer the long-running [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas "Indigenous peoples of the Americas") feature "American Eagle" in _Prize Comics Western_ vol. 9, #6 (Jan. 1951), inked by his high-school classmate turned fellow pro Will Elder.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-11)

Around this time, Severin did his first confirmed work for two publishers with whom he would long be associated, [Marvel Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvel_Comics "Marvel Comics") and [EC Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EC_Comics "EC Comics"). For the future Marvel Comics, he penciled the seven-page [romance comic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romance_comics "Romance comics") story "My Heart Had No Faith" in [Timely Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timely_Comics "Timely Comics")' _Actual Romances_ #1 (Oct. 1949).

### EC Comics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Severin&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: EC Comics")]

For EC Comics, he debuted with the seven-page "War Story" in _[Two-Fisted Tales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-Fisted\_Tales "Two-Fisted Tales")_ #19 (Feb. 1951), continuing to work in tandem with his friend Elder as his inker, notably on science fiction and war stories.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-gcd-10) Severin drew stories for both _Two-Fisted Tales_ and _[Frontline Combat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frontline\_Combat "Frontline Combat")_. When Kurtzman dropped the war comics to devote more time to _[Mad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mad\_(magazine) "Mad (magazine)")_, Severin became sole artist on _Two-Fisted Tales_ for four issues and scripted some stories. He also illustrated stories written by his friend [Colin Dawkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Dawkins "Colin Dawkins") and future _Mad_ art director [John Putnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Putnam_(comics) "John Putnam (comics)"). Severin and Dawkins were the uncredited co-editors of _Two-Fisted Tales_ #36–39.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-12)

Severin and Elder eventually split as a team at EC. They both were in the group of the five original artists who launched editor [Harvey Kurtzman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_Kurtzman "Harvey Kurtzman")'s landmark [satiric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satire "Satire") comic book _Mad_, along with Kurtzman, [Wally Wood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wally_Wood "Wally Wood") and [Jack Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Davis_(cartoonist) "Jack Davis (cartoonist)").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-13) Severin appeared in nine of _Mad'_ s first ten issues, drawing ten pieces between 1952 and 1954.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-14) According to accounts by both Severin and Kurtzman, the two had a falling out over art criticisms Kurtzman made during this period. It was Kurtzman who suggested that Severin ink with a pen as opposed to brush inking. Though Severin eventually took this advice in his later work, he was annoyed at Kurtzman at the time, for this and other remarks, and refused further work with him. Kurtzman insisted on doing the layouts for all the artists, which some resented, including Severin.

His ability to draw people of different nationalities convincingly was highly admired by his peers, as was his eye for authentic details.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-Schelly-15) Upon Severin's death, writer [Mark Evanier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Evanier "Mark Evanier") remembered, "[Jack Kirby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Kirby "Jack Kirby") used to say that when he had to research some historical costume or weapon for a story, it was just as good to use a John Severin drawing as it was to find a photo of the real thing. They don't make 'em like that anymore."[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-16)

### Marvel Comics and other publishers

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Severin&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Marvel Comics and other publishers")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/7/75/SgtFury57.jpg/250px-SgtFury57.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SgtFury57.jpg)

_Sgt. Fury and his Howling Commandos_ #57 (Aug. 1968). Cover art by [penciler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penciler "Penciler")[Dick Ayers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Ayers "Dick Ayers") and [inker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inker "Inker") Severin.

Following the cancellation of [EC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EC_Comics "EC Comics")'s comic book line in the wake of the [Comics Code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comics_Code "Comics Code") in the mid-1950s, Severin began working for [Atlas Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s) "Atlas Comics (1950s)"), the 1950s forerunner of [Marvel Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvel_Comics "Marvel Comics"). _Sergeant Barney Barker_, drawn by Severin, was Atlas' answer to _[Sgt. Bilko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Phil\_Silvers\_Show "The Phil Silvers Show")_.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-squa36-8):3[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-17) Artist and colorist [Stan Goldberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Goldberg "Stan Goldberg"), a company colleague, recalled in 2005,

> I was in the [company's artist room known as the] Bullpen with a lot of well-known artists who worked up there at that time. We had our Bullpen up there until about 1958 or 1959. [[sic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sic "Sic"); the Bullpen staff was let go in 1957] The guys ... who actually worked nine-to-five and put in a regular day, and not the freelance guys who'd come in a drop off their work ... were almost a hall-of-fame group of people. There was John Severin. [Bill Everett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Everett "Bill Everett"). [Carl Burgos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Burgos "Carl Burgos"). There was the all-time great [Joe Maneely](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Maneely "Joe Maneely") ... We all worked together, all the colorists and correction guys, the letterers and artists ... We had a great time.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-goldberg-18)

After Atlas transitioned to become Marvel Comics in the 1960s, Severin did extensive work as [penciler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penciler "Penciler"), [inker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inker "Inker") or both on such series as _[The Incredible Hulk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Incredible\_Hulk\_(comic\_book) "The Incredible Hulk (comic book)")_, _[Conan the Barbarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conan\_the\_Barbarian\_(comics) "Conan the Barbarian (comics)")_, and _[Captain Savage and his Leatherneck Raiders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain\_Savage\_and\_his\_Leatherneck\_Raiders "Captain Savage and his Leatherneck Raiders")_. [Herb Trimpe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Trimpe "Herb Trimpe"), the primary _Hulk_ penciler during this period comics fans and historians call the [Silver Age of comic books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_Age_of_comic_books "Silver Age of comic books"), said in 2009, "I was kind of thrilled when John Severin inked me, because I liked his work for EC Comics, and he was one of my idols."[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-19) As inker, Severin teamed with penciler [Dick Ayers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Ayers "Dick Ayers") on an acclaimed run of the [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") series _[Sgt. Fury and his Howling Commandos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sgt.\_Fury\_and\_his\_Howling\_Commandos "Sgt. Fury and his Howling Commandos")_, beginning with #44 (July 1967). In the 1970s, he collaborated with his sister, artist [Marie Severin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Severin "Marie Severin"), on Marvel's [sword and sorcery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sword_and_sorcery "Sword and sorcery") series, _[King Kull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kull\_of\_Atlantis "Kull of Atlantis")_.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-20)

During this time he was by far the most prolific contributor to the [satiric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satire "Satire")_[Cracked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cracked\_(magazine) "Cracked (magazine)")_ magazine, drawing television and movie parodies along with other features, including most of the magazine's covers. Severin was _Cracked'_ s signature artist for nearly 40 years.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

For [Warren Publishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Publishing "Warren Publishing") in the 1960s, he drew for the black-and-white comics magazines _[Blazing Combat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blazing\_Combat "Blazing Combat")_ and _[Creepy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creepy\_(magazine) "Creepy (magazine)")_. Severin also contributed to [Topps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topps "Topps")' line of bubble gum [trading cards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trading_cards "Trading cards").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-21) He was one of the artists on [Joe Kubert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Kubert "Joe Kubert")'s self-published _Sojourn_ series in 1977.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-22) His 1980s work for Marvel included _[The 'Nam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_'Nam "The 'Nam")_, _[What The--?!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What\_The--%3F! "What The--?!")_, _[Savage Tales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savage\_Tales "Savage Tales")_ (volume 2), and _[Semper Fi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semper\_Fi\_(comics)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Semper Fi (comics) (page does not exist)")_.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-23)

Circa 2000, writer [Jeff Mariotte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Mariotte "Jeff Mariotte") recalled in 2002, Severin phoned [Scott Dunbier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Dunbier "Scott Dunbier"), a group editor at [DC Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DC_Comics "DC Comics")' [WildStorm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WildStorm "WildStorm") imprint, "and said he was looking to do comics again" after working primarily for _Cracked_ at the time. "I happened to pass by Scott's office as he hung up the phone, and he sounded kind of awestruck as he told me that John Severin wanted to do something with us. I said something like, 'Gee, a _[Desperadoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desperadoes\_(comics) "Desperadoes (comics)")_ story by Severin would be great,'" referring to Mariotte's [Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_comics "Western comics") miniseries for DC. "Scott agreed. We needed to hurry, before he was snapped up by someone else, so I went home and worked up a proposal overnight. We had sent him, right after that first call, copies of the original _Desperadoes_ books. That was followed up by the proposal, the next day. He liked what he saw and wanted to play along."[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-scoop-mariotte-24) This led to Severin drawing the sequel miniseries _Desperadoes: Quiet of The Grave_.

He illustrated the controversial 2003 Marvel [limited series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limited_series_(comics) "Limited series (comics)")_[The Rawhide Kid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Rawhide\_Kid "The Rawhide Kid")_,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-25) a lighthearted [parallel universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallel_universe_(fiction) "Parallel universe (fiction)") Western that reimagined the outlaw hero as a [kitschy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kitschy "Kitschy") though still formidably gunslinging gay man. Severin, who had drawn the character for Atlas in the 1950s, refuted rumors that he had not known of the subject matter, saying at the time of the premiere issue's release, "The Rawhide Kid is rather effeminate in this story. It may be quite a blow to some of the old fans of Rawhide Kid. But it's a lot of fun, and he's still a tough _hombre_."[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-26) Also in the 2000s, Severin contributed to Marvel's _[The Punisher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punisher "Punisher")_; [DC Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DC_Comics "DC Comics")' _[Suicide Squad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suicide\_Squad "Suicide Squad")_, _[American Century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American\_Century\_(comics) "American Century (comics)")_, _Caper_, and _[Bat Lash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bat\_Lash "Bat Lash")_; and [Dark Horse Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_Horse_Comics "Dark Horse Comics")' _[Conan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conan\_(Dark\_Horse\_Comics) "Conan (Dark Horse Comics)")_, _[B.P.R.D.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B.P.R.D. "B.P.R.D.")_ and _[Witchfinder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellboy\_Universe#Sir\_Edward\_Grey,\_Witchfinder "Hellboy Universe")_.

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Severin&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Severin's family members working in the publishing and entertainment fields include his sister [Marie Severin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Severin "Marie Severin"), a comic book artist, who was the colorist for EC's comics; his son John Severin, Jr., the head of Bubblehead Publishing; his daughter, Ruth Larenas (d. 2023),[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-27) a producer for that company; and his grandson, John Severin III, a music producer and recording engineer.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-30)

Severin died at his home in [Denver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver "Denver"), Colorado, on February 12, 2012, at the age of 90. His wife of 60 years, Michelina, survived him, as did his six children and comics artist sister Marie Severin.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-32)

## Awards and honors

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Severin&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Awards and honors")]

Severin received an [Inkpot Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inkpot_Award "Inkpot Award") in 1998[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-33) and was inducted into the [Will Eisner Award Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Eisner_Award_winners#The_Will_Eisner_Award_Hall_of_Fame "List of Eisner Award winners") in 2003.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-34)

With writer [Gary Friedrich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Friedrich "Gary Friedrich") and penciler [Dick Ayers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Ayers "Dick Ayers"), Severin's inking contributed to _[Sgt. Fury and his Howling Commandos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sgt.\_Fury\_and\_his\_Howling\_Commandos "Sgt. Fury and his Howling Commandos")_ winning the [Alley Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alley_Award "Alley Award") for [Best War Title of 1967](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alley_Award#1967 "Alley Award") and [1968](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alley_Award#1968 "Alley Award").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-36)

He was among the winners of the [Cartoon Art Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartoon_Art_Museum "Cartoon Art Museum")'s 2001 Sparky Award.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-37)

His artwork was exhibited three times at the [Words & Pictures Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Words_&_Pictures_Museum "Words & Pictures Museum") in [Northampton, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northampton,_Massachusetts "Northampton, Massachusetts") – in the grand-opening group show (October 9, 1992 – January 5, 1993), in the group exhibit "War No More" (May 18 – August 8, 1993) and in the group show "Classic Comics: A Selection of Stories from EC Comics" (December 7 – February 11, 1996).[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-38)

In 2022, Severin was awarded the [Inkwell Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inkwell_Awards "Inkwell Awards") Stacey Aragon Special Achievement Award (SASRA) for his lifetime achievement in inking.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-39)

**John Powers Severin**[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-2) ([/ˈ s ɛ v ər ɪ n/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); December 26, 1921– February 12, 2012)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-4) was an American [comics artist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comics_artist "Comics artist") noted for his distinctive work with [EC Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EC_Comics "EC Comics"), primarily on the [war comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_comics "War comics")_[Two-Fisted Tales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-Fisted\_Tales "Two-Fisted Tales")_ and _[Frontline Combat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frontline\_Combat "Frontline Combat")_; for [Marvel Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvel_Comics "Marvel Comics"), especially its war and [Western comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_comics "Western comics"); and for his 45-year stint with the [satiric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satire "Satire") magazine _[Cracked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cracked\_(magazine) "Cracked (magazine)")_. He was one of the founding cartoonists of _[Mad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mad\_(magazine) "Mad (magazine)")_ in 1952.

Severin was inducted into the [Will Eisner Award Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Eisner_Award_winners#The_Will_Eisner_Award_Hall_of_Fame "List of Eisner Award winners") in 2003.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Severin&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

John Severin was born in [Jersey City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jersey_City,_New_Jersey "Jersey City, New Jersey"), New Jersey, of Norwegian and Irish descent. He was a teenager in [Bay Ridge, Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_Ridge,_Brooklyn "Bay Ridge, Brooklyn"), New York City, when he began drawing professionally. While attending high school, he contributed cartoons to _[The Hobo News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Hobo\_News "The Hobo News")_, receiving payment of one dollar per cartoon. Severin recalled in 1999:

> I was sometimes selling 19 or 20 of them a week. Not every week, naturally. But I didn't have to get a regular job to carry me through high school. It was almost every week—not every week—but almost every week. I didn't have to get a job. I hated to work, I'll tell you. I didn't have to get a job then, because I was in high school.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-5)

He attended the [High School of Music & Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_High_School_of_Music_&_Art "The High School of Music & Art") in New York City, together with future [EC Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EC_Comics "EC Comics") and _[Mad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mad\_(magazine) "Mad (magazine)")_ artists [Harvey Kurtzman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_Kurtzman "Harvey Kurtzman"), [Will Elder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Will_Elder "Will Elder"), [Al Jaffee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jaffee "Al Jaffee") and [Al Feldstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Feldstein "Al Feldstein").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-lam-6) After graduating from the school in 1940, he worked as an apprentice machinist and then enlisted in the [Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army "United States Army"), serving in the [Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_War "Pacific War") during World War II.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-7)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Severin&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### Early work: 1947–51

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Severin&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Early work: 1947–51")]

In a 1980 interview, Severin recalled his start as a professional artist:

> I had decided to exhibit some paintings of mine in a High School of Music and Art exhibition for the alumni. Charlie Stern was in charge of it, so I went to see him at his studio. He was the "Charles" of the Charles William Harvey Studio, the other two being William Elder and Harvey Kurtzman. They asked me if I'd like to rent space with them there. I did, and started working with them. When Charlie left ... I became the third man, but they didn't want to change it to John William Harvey Studio, so they left the name ... Harvey was doing comics, Willie and Charlie were doing advertising stuff, and I just joined in ... [I did] design work, logos for toy boxes, logos for candy boxes, cards to be included in the candy boxes.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-squa36-8)

Inspired by the quick money Kurtzman would make in between advertising assignments with one-page "Hey Look!" gags for editor [Stan Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Lee "Stan Lee") at [Timely Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timely_Comics "Timely Comics"), Severin worked up comics samples inked by Elder. In late 1947, he recalled, the writer-artist-editor team of [Joe Simon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Simon "Joe Simon") and [Jack Kirby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Kirby "Jack Kirby") at [Crestwood Publications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crestwood_Publications "Crestwood Publications") "gave us our first job."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-squa36-8)

Since it was not standard practice to credit comics creators during this era, a comprehensive list of his early work is difficult to compile. Author and historian Jim Vadeboncoeur Jr., based on Severin's description of "a crime story about a boy and a girl who killed somebody ... I think it was their stepfather. They lived on a farm, or out in the suburbs," believes that first Severin/Elder story was the eight-page "The Clue of the Horoscope" in _Headline Comics_ #32 ([cover-dated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cover-date "Cover-date") Nov. 1948), from the Crestwood-affiliated [Prize Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prize_Comics "Prize Comics").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-squa36-8) The standard reference [Grand Comics Database](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Comics_Database "Grand Comics Database") has no credits for that story,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-9) and lists Severin's first confirmed work in comics as two stories published the same month: the ten-page [Boy Commandos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boy_Commandos "Boy Commandos") adventure "The Triumph of William Tell" in [DC Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DC_Comics "DC Comics")' _Boy Commandos_ #30; and the eight-page [Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_comics "Western comics") story "Grinning Hole in the Wall" in Prize Comics' _Prize Comics Western_ vol. 7, #5 (each Dec. 1948), both of which he [penciled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penciler "Penciler") and the latter of which he also [inked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inker "Inker").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-gcd-10)

Through 1955, Severin drew a large number of stories for the latter title and other Western series from Prize, and as penciler, he co-created with an unknown writer the long-running [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas "Indigenous peoples of the Americas") feature "American Eagle" in _Prize Comics Western_ vol. 9, #6 (Jan. 1951), inked by his high-school classmate turned fellow pro Will Elder.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-11)

Around this time, Severin did his first confirmed work for two publishers with whom he would long be associated, [Marvel Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvel_Comics "Marvel Comics") and [EC Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EC_Comics "EC Comics"). For the future Marvel Comics, he penciled the seven-page [romance comic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romance_comics "Romance comics") story "My Heart Had No Faith" in [Timely Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timely_Comics "Timely Comics")' _Actual Romances_ #1 (Oct. 1949).

### EC Comics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Severin&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: EC Comics")]

For EC Comics, he debuted with the seven-page "War Story" in _[Two-Fisted Tales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-Fisted\_Tales "Two-Fisted Tales")_ #19 (Feb. 1951), continuing to work in tandem with his friend Elder as his inker, notably on science fiction and war stories.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-gcd-10) Severin drew stories for both _Two-Fisted Tales_ and _[Frontline Combat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frontline\_Combat "Frontline Combat")_. When Kurtzman dropped the war comics to devote more time to _[Mad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mad\_(magazine) "Mad (magazine)")_, Severin became sole artist on _Two-Fisted Tales_ for four issues and scripted some stories. He also illustrated stories written by his friend [Colin Dawkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Dawkins "Colin Dawkins") and future _Mad_ art director [John Putnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Putnam_(comics) "John Putnam (comics)"). Severin and Dawkins were the uncredited co-editors of _Two-Fisted Tales_ #36–39.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-12)

Severin and Elder eventually split as a team at EC. They both were in the group of the five original artists who launched editor [Harvey Kurtzman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_Kurtzman "Harvey Kurtzman")'s landmark [satiric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satire "Satire") comic book _Mad_, along with Kurtzman, [Wally Wood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wally_Wood "Wally Wood") and [Jack Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Davis_(cartoonist) "Jack Davis (cartoonist)").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-13) Severin appeared in nine of _Mad'_ s first ten issues, drawing ten pieces between 1952 and 1954.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-14) According to accounts by both Severin and Kurtzman, the two had a falling out over art criticisms Kurtzman made during this period. It was Kurtzman who suggested that Severin ink with a pen as opposed to brush inking. Though Severin eventually took this advice in his later work, he was annoyed at Kurtzman at the time, for this and other remarks, and refused further work with him. Kurtzman insisted on doing the layouts for all the artists, which some resented, including Severin.

His ability to draw people of different nationalities convincingly was highly admired by his peers, as was his eye for authentic details.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-Schelly-15) Upon Severin's death, writer [Mark Evanier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Evanier "Mark Evanier") remembered, "[Jack Kirby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Kirby "Jack Kirby") used to say that when he had to research some historical costume or weapon for a story, it was just as good to use a John Severin drawing as it was to find a photo of the real thing. They don't make 'em like that anymore."[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-16)

### Marvel Comics and other publishers

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Severin&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Marvel Comics and other publishers")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/7/75/SgtFury57.jpg/250px-SgtFury57.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SgtFury57.jpg)

_Sgt. Fury and his Howling Commandos_ #57 (Aug. 1968). Cover art by [penciler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penciler "Penciler")[Dick Ayers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Ayers "Dick Ayers") and [inker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inker "Inker") Severin.

Following the cancellation of [EC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EC_Comics "EC Comics")'s comic book line in the wake of the [Comics Code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comics_Code "Comics Code") in the mid-1950s, Severin began working for [Atlas Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s) "Atlas Comics (1950s)"), the 1950s forerunner of [Marvel Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvel_Comics "Marvel Comics"). _Sergeant Barney Barker_, drawn by Severin, was Atlas' answer to _[Sgt. Bilko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Phil\_Silvers\_Show "The Phil Silvers Show")_.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-squa36-8):3[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-17) Artist and colorist [Stan Goldberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Goldberg "Stan Goldberg"), a company colleague, recalled in 2005,

> I was in the [company's artist room known as the] Bullpen with a lot of well-known artists who worked up there at that time. We had our Bullpen up there until about 1958 or 1959. [[sic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sic "Sic"); the Bullpen staff was let go in 1957] The guys ... who actually worked nine-to-five and put in a regular day, and not the freelance guys who'd come in a drop off their work ... were almost a hall-of-fame group of people. There was John Severin. [Bill Everett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Everett "Bill Everett"). [Carl Burgos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Burgos "Carl Burgos"). There was the all-time great [Joe Maneely](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Maneely "Joe Maneely") ... We all worked together, all the colorists and correction guys, the letterers and artists ... We had a great time.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-goldberg-18)

After Atlas transitioned to become Marvel Comics in the 1960s, Severin did extensive work as [penciler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penciler "Penciler"), [inker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inker "Inker") or both on such series as _[The Incredible Hulk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Incredible\_Hulk\_(comic\_book) "The Incredible Hulk (comic book)")_, _[Conan the Barbarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conan\_the\_Barbarian\_(comics) "Conan the Barbarian (comics)")_, and _[Captain Savage and his Leatherneck Raiders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain\_Savage\_and\_his\_Leatherneck\_Raiders "Captain Savage and his Leatherneck Raiders")_. [Herb Trimpe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Trimpe "Herb Trimpe"), the primary _Hulk_ penciler during this period comics fans and historians call the [Silver Age of comic books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_Age_of_comic_books "Silver Age of comic books"), said in 2009, "I was kind of thrilled when John Severin inked me, because I liked his work for EC Comics, and he was one of my idols."[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-19) As inker, Severin teamed with penciler [Dick Ayers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Ayers "Dick Ayers") on an acclaimed run of the [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") series _[Sgt. Fury and his Howling Commandos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sgt.\_Fury\_and\_his\_Howling\_Commandos "Sgt. Fury and his Howling Commandos")_, beginning with #44 (July 1967). In the 1970s, he collaborated with his sister, artist [Marie Severin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Severin "Marie Severin"), on Marvel's [sword and sorcery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sword_and_sorcery "Sword and sorcery") series, _[King Kull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kull\_of\_Atlantis "Kull of Atlantis")_.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-20)

During this time he was by far the most prolific contributor to the [satiric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satire "Satire")_[Cracked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cracked\_(magazine) "Cracked (magazine)")_ magazine, drawing television and movie parodies along with other features, including most of the magazine's covers. Severin was _Cracked'_ s signature artist for nearly 40 years.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

For [Warren Publishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Publishing "Warren Publishing") in the 1960s, he drew for the black-and-white comics magazines _[Blazing Combat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blazing\_Combat "Blazing Combat")_ and _[Creepy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creepy\_(magazine) "Creepy (magazine)")_. Severin also contributed to [Topps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topps "Topps")' line of bubble gum [trading cards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trading_cards "Trading cards").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-21) He was one of the artists on [Joe Kubert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Kubert "Joe Kubert")'s self-published _Sojourn_ series in 1977.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-22) His 1980s work for Marvel included _[The 'Nam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_'Nam "The 'Nam")_, _[What The--?!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What\_The--%3F! "What The--?!")_, _[Savage Tales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savage\_Tales "Savage Tales")_ (volume 2), and _[Semper Fi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semper\_Fi\_(comics)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Semper Fi (comics) (page does not exist)")_.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-23)

Circa 2000, writer [Jeff Mariotte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Mariotte "Jeff Mariotte") recalled in 2002, Severin phoned [Scott Dunbier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Dunbier "Scott Dunbier"), a group editor at [DC Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DC_Comics "DC Comics")' [WildStorm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WildStorm "WildStorm") imprint, "and said he was looking to do comics again" after working primarily for _Cracked_ at the time. "I happened to pass by Scott's office as he hung up the phone, and he sounded kind of awestruck as he told me that John Severin wanted to do something with us. I said something like, 'Gee, a _[Desperadoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desperadoes\_(comics) "Desperadoes (comics)")_ story by Severin would be great,'" referring to Mariotte's [Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_comics "Western comics") miniseries for DC. "Scott agreed. We needed to hurry, before he was snapped up by someone else, so I went home and worked up a proposal overnight. We had sent him, right after that first call, copies of the original _Desperadoes_ books. That was followed up by the proposal, the next day. He liked what he saw and wanted to play along."[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-scoop-mariotte-24) This led to Severin drawing the sequel miniseries _Desperadoes: Quiet of The Grave_.

He illustrated the controversial 2003 Marvel [limited series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limited_series_(comics) "Limited series (comics)")_[The Rawhide Kid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Rawhide\_Kid "The Rawhide Kid")_,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-25) a lighthearted [parallel universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallel_universe_(fiction) "Parallel universe (fiction)") Western that reimagined the outlaw hero as a [kitschy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kitschy "Kitschy") though still formidably gunslinging gay man. Severin, who had drawn the character for Atlas in the 1950s, refuted rumors that he had not known of the subject matter, saying at the time of the premiere issue's release, "The Rawhide Kid is rather effeminate in this story. It may be quite a blow to some of the old fans of Rawhide Kid. But it's a lot of fun, and he's still a tough _hombre_."[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-26) Also in the 2000s, Severin contributed to Marvel's _[The Punisher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punisher "Punisher")_; [DC Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DC_Comics "DC Comics")' _[Suicide Squad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suicide\_Squad "Suicide Squad")_, _[American Century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American\_Century\_(comics) "American Century (comics)")_, _Caper_, and _[Bat Lash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bat\_Lash "Bat Lash")_; and [Dark Horse Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_Horse_Comics "Dark Horse Comics")' _[Conan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conan\_(Dark\_Horse\_Comics) "Conan (Dark Horse Comics)")_, _[B.P.R.D.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B.P.R.D. "B.P.R.D.")_ and _[Witchfinder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellboy\_Universe#Sir\_Edward\_Grey,\_Witchfinder "Hellboy Universe")_.

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Severin&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Severin's family members working in the publishing and entertainment fields include his sister [Marie Severin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Severin "Marie Severin"), a comic book artist, who was the colorist for EC's comics; his son John Severin, Jr., the head of Bubblehead Publishing; his daughter, Ruth Larenas (d. 2023),[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-27) a producer for that company; and his grandson, John Severin III, a music producer and recording engineer.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-30)

Severin died at his home in [Denver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver "Denver"), Colorado, on February 12, 2012, at the age of 90. His wife of 60 years, Michelina, survived him, as did his six children and comics artist sister Marie Severin.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-32)

## Awards and honors

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Severin&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Awards and honors")]

Severin received an [Inkpot Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inkpot_Award "Inkpot Award") in 1998[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-33) and was inducted into the [Will Eisner Award Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Eisner_Award_winners#The_Will_Eisner_Award_Hall_of_Fame "List of Eisner Award winners") in 2003.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-34)

With writer [Gary Friedrich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Friedrich "Gary Friedrich") and penciler [Dick Ayers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Ayers "Dick Ayers"), Severin's inking contributed to _[Sgt. Fury and his Howling Commandos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sgt.\_Fury\_and\_his\_Howling\_Commandos "Sgt. Fury and his Howling Commandos")_ winning the [Alley Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alley_Award "Alley Award") for [Best War Title of 1967](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alley_Award#1967 "Alley Award") and [1968](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alley_Award#1968 "Alley Award").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-36)

He was among the winners of the [Cartoon Art Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartoon_Art_Museum "Cartoon Art Museum")'s 2001 Sparky Award.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-37)

His artwork was exhibited three times at the [Words & Pictures Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Words_&_Pictures_Museum "Words & Pictures Museum") in [Northampton, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northampton,_Massachusetts "Northampton, Massachusetts") – in the grand-opening group show (October 9, 1992 – January 5, 1993), in the group exhibit "War No More" (May 18 – August 8, 1993) and in the group show "Classic Comics: A Selection of Stories from EC Comics" (December 7 – February 11, 1996).[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-38)

In 2022, Severin was awarded the [Inkwell Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inkwell_Awards "Inkwell Awards") Stacey Aragon Special Achievement Award (SASRA) for his lifetime achievement in inking.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Severin#cite_note-39)
