From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

US comic book publisher (1951–1957)

Atlas Comics[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/Atlas_Comics_logo.svg/250px-Atlas_Comics_logo.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Atlas_Comics_logo.svg)
Type[Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Division_(business) "Division (business)")
Industry[Publishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishing "Publishing")
Predecessor[Timely Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timely_Comics "Timely Comics")
Founded November 1951;74 years ago(1951-11)
Founder[Martin Goodman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Goodman_(publisher) "Martin Goodman (publisher)")
Defunct October 1957;68 years ago(1957-10)
Fate Rebranded as [Marvel Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvel_Comics "Marvel Comics") in 1961
Successor Marvel Comics
Headquarters[Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan"), [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), U.S.
Key people[Martin Goodman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Goodman_(publisher) "Martin Goodman (publisher)")
Products[Comic books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comic_book "Comic book"), [magazines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magazines "Magazines")
[Parent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parent_company "Parent company")[Magazine Management Co., Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magazine_Management_Co.,_Inc. "Magazine Management Co., Inc.")

**Atlas Comics** was the 1950s [comic-book](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comic_book "Comic book")[publishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishing "Publishing") label that evolved into [Marvel Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvel_Comics "Marvel Comics").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-1) Magazine and [paperback novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_market_paperback "Mass market paperback") publisher [Martin Goodman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Goodman_(publisher) "Martin Goodman (publisher)"), whose business strategy involved having a multitude of corporate entities, used Atlas as the umbrella name for his comic book division during this time. Atlas evolved out of Goodman's 1940s comic book division, [Timely Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timely_Comics "Timely Comics"), and was located on the 14th floor of the [Empire State Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_State_Building "Empire State Building"). This company is distinct from the 1970s comic-book company, also founded by Goodman, that is known as [Atlas/Seaboard Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas/Seaboard_Comics "Atlas/Seaboard Comics").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atlas_Comics_(1950s)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### After the Golden Age

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atlas_Comics_(1950s)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: After the Golden Age")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/6/64/YoungMen25.jpg/250px-YoungMen25.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:YoungMen25.jpg)

_Young Men_ #25 (Feb. 1954): Cover art by [Carl Burgos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Burgos "Carl Burgos").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-2) Note the Atlas globe in the top left corner.

Atlas Comics was the successor of [Timely Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timely_Comics "Timely Comics"), the company that [magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magazine "Magazine") and [paperback novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_market_paperback "Mass market paperback") publisher Martin Goodman founded in 1939, and which had reached the peak of its popularity during the war years with its star characters the [Human Torch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Torch_(Golden_Age) "Human Torch (Golden Age)"), the [Sub-Mariner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Namor_the_Sub-Mariner "Namor the Sub-Mariner") and [Captain America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_America "Captain America").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-3) The early to mid-1950s found comic books falling out of fashion due to competition from [television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television "Television") and other media.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-4)

Timely largely stopped producing superhero comics with the cancellation of _[Captain America Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain\_America\_Comics "Captain America Comics")_ at issue #75 ([cover-dated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cover-date "Cover-date") Feb. 1950), by which time the series had already been titled _[Captain America's Weird Tales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain\_America's\_Weird\_Tales "Captain America's Weird Tales")_ for two issues, with the finale featuring only anthological [suspense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suspense "Suspense") stories and no superheroes.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-5) The company's flagship title, _[Marvel Mystery Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvel\_Mystery\_Comics "Marvel Mystery Comics")_, starring the Human Torch, had already ended its run with #92 in June 1949,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-gcd-marvelmystery-6) as had _Sub-Mariner Comics_ with #32 the same month,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-gcd-GAsubmariner-7) and _The Human Torch_ with #35 in March 1949.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-gcd-GAHumanTorch-8) Timely made one more attempt at superheroes with the publication of _Marvel Boy_ #1-2 (Dec. 1950 - Feb. 1951),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-Brevoort-9):7 which was retitled _Astonishing_ with issue #3 (April 1951) and continued the _Marvel Boy_ feature through #6 (Oct. 1951).[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-11)

In the absence of superheroes, Goodman's comic book line expanded into a wide variety of genres, producing [horror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horror_comics "Horror comics"), [Westerns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_comics "Western comics"), [humor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humour "Humour"), [talking animal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talking_animals_in_fiction "Talking animals in fiction"), [drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drama "Drama"), [crime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crime_fiction "Crime fiction"), [war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_comics "War comics"), [jungle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jungle "Jungle"), [romance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romance_comics "Romance comics"), [espionage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spy_fiction "Spy fiction"), [medieval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages "Middle Ages") adventure, [Bible stories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bible_story "Bible story") and [sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sport "Sport") comics. As did other publishers, Atlas also offered comics about [models](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Model_(people) "Model (people)") and career women.

Goodman began using the logo of the Atlas News Company, the newsstand-distribution company he owned, on comics [cover-dated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cover-date "Cover-date") November 1951, even though another company, Kable News, continued to distribute his comics through the August 1952 issues, with its "K" logo and the logo of the independent distributors' union appearing alongside the Atlas globe.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-gcdatlasglobe-12) The Atlas logo united a line put out by the same publisher, staff and freelancers through 59 shell companies, from Animirth Comics to Zenith Publications.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-13) Soon afterwards, the company rejoined the [Association of Comics Magazine Publishers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Comics_Magazine_Publishers "Association of Comics Magazine Publishers") and begin using the "star" logo of ACMP on comics cover-dated between April 1952 and January 1955 on its titles, prior to the establishment of the [Comics Code Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comics_Code_Authority "Comics Code Authority").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-15)

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/8/83/Atlas_interior_logo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Atlas_interior_logo.jpg)

The logo treatment on a 1954 comic-book page, with "Atlas" as the comics brand

Atlas attempted to revive superheroes in _Young Men_ #24-28 (Dec. 1953 - June 1954) with the Human Torch (art by [Syd Shores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syd_Shores "Syd Shores") and [Dick Ayers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Ayers "Dick Ayers"), variously), the Sub-Mariner (drawn and most stories written by [Bill Everett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Everett "Bill Everett")) and [Captain America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_America "Captain America") (writer [Stan Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Lee "Stan Lee"), artist [John Romita Sr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Romita_Sr. "John Romita Sr.")). The short-lived revival also included restarts of _Sub-Mariner Comics_ (issues #33-42, April 1954 - Oct. 1955)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-16) and _Captain America_ (#76-78, May-Sept. 1954).[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-17) All three superheroes also appeared in the final two issues of _Men's Adventures_ (#27-28, May–July 1954).[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-18)

### Trend-following

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atlas_Comics_(1950s)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Trend-following")]

[![Image 7](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/6/6f/Astonishing30.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Astonishing30.jpg)

The pre-[Comics Code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comics_Code "Comics Code")_Astonishing_ #30 (Feb. 1954): Cover art by [Joe Maneely](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Maneely "Joe Maneely").

Goodman's publishing strategy for Atlas involved what he saw as the proven route of following popular trends in TV and [movies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movies "Movies") — [Westerns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_fiction "Western fiction") and war dramas prevailing for a time, [drive-in](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drive-in "Drive-in")[movie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movie "Movie") monsters another time — and even other comic books, particularly the [EC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertaining_Comics "Entertaining Comics")[horror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horror_(genre) "Horror (genre)") line.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-Daniels-20):67–68 As Marvel/Atlas editor-in-chief [Stan Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Lee "Stan Lee") told comic-book historian [Les Daniels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_Daniels "Les Daniels"), Goodman "would notice what was selling, and we'd put out a lot of books of that type." Commented Daniels, "The short-term results were lucrative; but while other publishers took the long view and kept their stables of heroes solid, Goodman let his slide."[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-Daniels-20):57

While Atlas had some horror titles, such as _[Marvel Tales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvel\_Tales\_(1949%E2%80%931957) "Marvel Tales (1949–1957)")_, as far back as 1949, the company increased its output dramatically in the wake of EC's success. Lee recalled, "[I]t was usually based on how the competition was doing. When we found that EC's horror books were doing well, for instance, we published a lot of horror books."[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-Daniels-20):67–68 Until the early 1960s, when Lee, [Jack Kirby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Kirby "Jack Kirby") and [Steve Ditko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Ditko "Steve Ditko") would help revolutionize comic books with the advent of the [Fantastic Four](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fantastic_Four "Fantastic Four") and [Spider-Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spider-Man "Spider-Man"), Atlas was content to flood newsstands with profitable, cheaply produced product — often, despite itself, beautifully rendered by talented if low-paid artists.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-21)

The Atlas "bullpen" had at least five staff writers (officially called editors) besides Lee: [Hank Chapman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hank_Chapman "Hank Chapman"), [Paul S. Newman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_S._Newman "Paul S. Newman"), [Don Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Rico "Don Rico"), [Carl Wessler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Wessler "Carl Wessler"), and, in the teen humor division, future _[Mad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mad\_(magazine) "Mad (magazine)")_ magazine cartoonist [Al Jaffee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jaffee "Al Jaffee"). [Daniel Keyes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Keyes "Daniel Keyes"), future author of _[Flowers for Algernon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flowers\_for\_Algernon "Flowers for Algernon")_, was an  editor beginning 1952.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-autobiop79-80-22) Other writers, generally freelance, included [Robert Bernstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Bernstein_(comics) "Robert Bernstein (comics)").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-bernsteingcd-23)

The artists — some freelance, some on staff — included such veterans as Human Torch creator [Carl Burgos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Burgos "Carl Burgos")[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-burgosgcd-24) and Sub-Mariner creator [Bill Everett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Everett "Bill Everett").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-gcd2-25) The next generation included the prolific and much-admired [Joe Maneely](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Maneely "Joe Maneely"), who before his death just prior to Marvel's 1960s breakthrough was the company's leading artist,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-26) providing many covers and doing work in all genres, most notably on Westerns and on the medieval adventure _[Black Knight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black\_Knight\_(Sir\_Percy) "Black Knight (Sir Percy)")_.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-gcd-joemaneely-27) Others included [Russ Heath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russ_Heath "Russ Heath"),[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-heathgcd-28)[Gene Colan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_Colan "Gene Colan"),[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-gcd-29) and the fledgling, highly individualistic [Steve Ditko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Ditko "Steve Ditko").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-ditkogcd-30)

Some of Atlas' prominent [Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_comics "Western comics") titles, many reprinted in the 1970s, were _[Ringo Kid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ringo\_Kid "Ringo Kid")_, with art by Maneely, [Fred Kida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Kida "Fred Kida") and John Severin; artist [Doug Wildey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doug_Wildey "Doug Wildey")'s _[The Outlaw Kid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outlaw\_Kid "Outlaw Kid")_; artist [Jack Keller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Keller_(comics) "Jack Keller (comics)")'s _[Kid Colt, Outlaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kid\_Colt,\_Outlaw "Kid Colt, Outlaw")_; the anthology _[Gunsmoke Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunsmoke\_Western "Gunsmoke Western")_, starring Kid Colt; and _[Black Rider](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black\_Rider\_(character) "Black Rider (character)")_, drawn by Maneely, [Syd Shores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syd_Shores "Syd Shores") and others.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-31)

### Humor and miscellanea

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atlas_Comics_(1950s)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Humor and miscellanea")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/f/f9/SgtBarneyBarker1.jpg/250px-SgtBarneyBarker1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SgtBarneyBarker1.jpg)

_Sergeant Barney Barker_ #1 (August. 1956), cover art by John Severin.

Atlas also published various children's and teen humor titles, including [Dan DeCarlo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_DeCarlo "Dan DeCarlo")'s _Homer, the Happy Ghost_ (a la _[Casper the Friendly Ghost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casper\_the\_Friendly\_Ghost "Casper the Friendly Ghost")_), _Homer Hooper_ (a la [Archie Andrews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Andrews "Archie Andrews")) and the [Joe Maneely](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Maneely "Joe Maneely")-drawn _Melvin the Monster_ (a la _[Dennis the Menace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennis\_the\_Menace\_(U.S.) "Dennis the Menace (U.S.)")_). _Sergeant Barney Barker_, drawn by John Severin, was Atlas' answer to _[Sgt. Bilko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Phil\_Silvers\_Show "The Phil Silvers Show")_.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-squa36-32)

One of the most long-running titles was _[Millie the Model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millie\_the\_Model "Millie the Model")_, which began as a Timely Comics humor series in 1945 and ran into the 1970s, lasting for 207 issues and launching spinoffs along the way. Created by writer-artist [Ruth Atkinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Atkinson "Ruth Atkinson"),[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-Manning-33):31 it later became the training ground for [cartoonist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartoonist "Cartoonist") DeCarlo — the future creator of _[Josie and the Pussycats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josie\_and\_the\_Pussycats\_(comic) "Josie and the Pussycats (comic)")_, _[Sabrina, the Teenage Witch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabrina,\_the\_Teenage\_Witch "Sabrina, the Teenage Witch")_ and other [Archie Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Comics "Archie Comics") characters, and the artist who established Archie Comics’ modern look.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-Manning-33):31[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-34) DeCarlo wrote and drew _Millie_ for 10 years.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-decarlogcd-35)

The high-school series _[Patsy Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patsy\_Walker\_(comic\_book) "Patsy Walker (comic book)")_, co-created by Atkinson and writer [Otto Binder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Binder "Otto Binder") in 1944,[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-36) featured art by [Al Hartley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Hartley "Al Hartley"), [Al Jaffee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jaffee "Al Jaffee"), [Morris Weiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Weiss "Morris Weiss") and others, and ran until 1967[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-37) It spun off three titles. Patsy herself would be integrated into [Marvel Universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvel_Universe "Marvel Universe") continuity years later as the [supernatural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supernatural "Supernatural") superheroine [Hellcat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellcat_(comics) "Hellcat (comics)").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-38)

Atlas' talking animal books featured [cartoonist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartoonist "Cartoonist")[Ed Winiarski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Winiarski "Ed Winiarski")'s trouble-prone _Buck Duck_, Maneely's mentally suspect _Dippy Duck_, and [Howie Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howie_Post "Howie Post")'s _The Monkey and the Bear_. Buck and the other animal characters briefly returned in the early 1970s when Marvel published the five-issue reprint title _Li'l Pals_ ("Fun-Filled Animal Antics!").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-lilpalsgcd-39)

Miscellaneous titles included the espionage series _[Yellow Claw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow\_Claw\_(character) "Yellow Claw (character)")_, with Maneely, Severin, and [Jack Kirby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Kirby "Jack Kirby") art; the [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Americans_in_the_United_States "Native Americans in the United States") hero _Red Warrior_, with art by [Tom Gill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Gill_(comics) "Tom Gill (comics)");[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-gillgcd-40) the [space opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_opera "Space opera")_Space Squadron_, written and drawn by future Marvel production executive [Sol Brodsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sol_Brodsky "Sol Brodsky");[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-brodskygcd-41) and _Sports Action_, initially featuring true-life stories about the likes of [George Gipp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Gipp "George Gipp") and [Jackie Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Robinson "Jackie Robinson"), and later fictional features of, as one cover headline put it, "Rugged Tales of Danger and Red-Hot Action!".[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-sportsactiongcd-42)

Staff artist [Stan Goldberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Goldberg "Stan Goldberg") recalled in 2005, "I was in the Bullpen with a lot of well-known artists who worked up there at that time. ... The guys ... who actually worked nine-to-five and put in a regular day, and not the freelance guys who'd come in a drop off their work ... were almost a hall of fame group of people. There was John Severin. [Bill Everett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Everett "Bill Everett"). [Carl Burgos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Burgos "Carl Burgos"). There was the all-time great Joe Maneely.... We all worked together, all the colorists and correction guys, the letterers and artists. ... We had a great time".[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-goldberg-43)

### Layoffs

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atlas_Comics_(1950s)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Layoffs")]

From 1952 to late 1956, Goodman distributed Atlas' comics to newsstands through his self-owned distributor, the Atlas News Company. He shut down Atlas News Company in 1956 and began newsstand distribution through [American News Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_News_Company "American News Company"),[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-gcdatlasglobe-12)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-Manning-33):66 the nation's largest distributor and a virtual [monopoly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monopoly "Monopoly"), which shortly afterward lost a [Justice Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Justice "United States Department of Justice")[lawsuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawsuit "Lawsuit") and discontinued its business. As comic-book historian [Gerard Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerard_Jones "Gerard Jones") explains, the company in 1956

> ...had been found guilty of restraint of trade and ordered to divest itself of the newsstands it owned. Its biggest client, [George Delacorte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Delacorte "George Delacorte"), announced he would seek a new distributor for his [Dell Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dell_Comics "Dell Comics") and paperbacks. The owners of American News estimated the effect that would have on their income. Then they looked at the value of the [New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey "New Jersey") real estate where their headquarters sat. They liquidated the company and sold the land. The company ... vanished without a trace in the [suburban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suburban "Suburban") growth of the 1950s.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-44)[_[page needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing\_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_]

The Atlas globe remained on the covers, however, until American News went out of business in June 1957.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-45) With no other options, Goodman turned to the distributor [Independent News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_News "Independent News"), owned by rival [National Periodical Publications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Periodical_Publications "National Periodical Publications"), the future [DC Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DC_Comics "DC Comics"), which agreed to distribute him on constrained terms that allowed only eight titles per month.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-Manning-33):66 The last comic to bear the Atlas globe on the cover was the comic _Dippy Duck_ #1,[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-46) and the first to bear the new "Ind." distributors' mark was _[Patsy Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patsy\_Walker\_(comic\_book) "Patsy Walker (comic book)")_ #73, both [cover-dated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cover-date "Cover-date") October 1957.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-47) The company was accordingly renamed to Goodman Comics after signing a distribution pact with [Independent News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_News "Independent News"), according to a 1960 trade article.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-48)

Stan Lee, in a 1988 interview, recalled that Goodman:

> ...had gone with the American News Company. I remember saying to him, 'Gee, why did you do that? I thought that we had a good distribution company.' His answer was like, 'Oh, Stan, you wouldn't understand. It has to do with finance.' I didn't really give a damn, and I went back to doing the comics. [Later,] we were left without a distributor and we couldn't go back to distributing our own books because the fact that Martin quit doing it and went with American News had gotten the wholesalers very angry ... and it would have been impossible for Martin to just say, 'Okay, we'll go back to where we were and distribute our books.' [We had been] turning out 40, 50, 60 books a month, maybe more, and [now] the only company we could get to distribute our books was our closest rival, National [DC] Comics. Suddenly we went ... to either eight or 12 books a month, which was all Independent News Distributors would accept from us.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-Stan_and_Roy-49)

During this retrenchment, according to a fabled industry story, Goodman discovered a closet-full of unused, but paid-for, art, leading him to have virtually the entire staff fired while he used up the inventory. In the interview noted above, Lee, one of the few able to give a firsthand account, told a seemingly self-contradictory version of the downsizing:

> It would never have happened just because he opened a closet door. But I think that I may have been in a little trouble when that happened. We had bought a lot of strips that I didn't think were really all that good, but I paid the artists and writers for them anyway, and I kinda hid them in the closet! And Martin found them and I think he wasn't too happy. If I wasn't satisfied with the work, I wasn't supposed to have paid, but I was never sure it was really the artist's or the writer's fault. But when the job was finished I didn't think that it was anything that I wanted to use. I felt that we could use it in inventory — put it out in other books. Martin, probably rightly so, was a little annoyed because it was his money I was spending.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-Stan_and_Roy-49)

In a 2003 interview, [Joe Sinnott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Sinnott "Joe Sinnott"), one of the company's top artists for more than 50 years, recalled Lee citing the inventory issue as a primary cause. "Stan called me and said, 'Joe, Martin Goodman told me to suspend operations because I have all this artwork in house and have to use it up before I can hire you again.' It turned out to be six months, in my case. He may have called back some of the other artists later, but that's what happened with me."[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-50)

### Pre-superhero Marvel

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atlas_Comics_(1950s)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Pre-superhero Marvel")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/92/StrangeWorlds1_Marvel.jpg/250px-StrangeWorlds1_Marvel.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:StrangeWorlds1_Marvel.jpg)

_[Strange Worlds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strange\_Worlds\_(Atlas\_Comics) "Strange Worlds (Atlas Comics)")_ #1 (Dec. 1958), the first Marvel/Atlas work by artist [Jack Kirby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Kirby "Jack Kirby") upon his permanent return to the company. Cover art by [penciler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penciler "Penciler") Kirby and [inker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inker "Inker")[Christopher Rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Rule "Christopher Rule").

Goodman's men's magazines and paperback books were still successful — the comics, except in the early Golden Age, were a relatively small part of the business — and Goodman considered shutting the division down. The details of his decision not to do so are murky. Artist [Jack Kirby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Kirby "Jack Kirby") — who had amicably split with creative partner [Joe Simon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Simon "Joe Simon") a few years earlier, and separately lost a lawsuit to a [DC Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DC_Comics "DC Comics") editor — was having difficulty finding work. He recalled that in late 1958,

> I came in [to the Marvel offices] and they were moving out the furniture, they were taking desks out — and I needed the work! ... Stan Lee is sitting on a chair crying. He didn't know what to do, he's sitting on a chair crying — he was still just out of his adolescence [Note: Lee, born Dec. 28, 1922, would actually have been about 36.] I told him to stop crying. I says, 'Go in to Martin and tell him to stop moving the furniture out, and I'll see that the books make money'.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-51)

The interviewer, _[The Comics Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Comics\_Journal "The Comics Journal")_ publisher [Gary Groth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Groth "Gary Groth"), later wrote of this interview in general, "Some of Kirby's more extreme statements ... should be taken with a grain of salt...."[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-52) Lee, specifically asked about the office-closing anecdote, said,

> I never remember being there when people were moving out the furniture. If they ever moved the furniture, they did it during the weekend when everybody was home. Jack tended toward hyperbole, just like the time he was quoted as saying that he came in and I was crying and I said, 'Please save the company!' I'm not a crier and I would never have said that. I was very happy that Jack was there and I loved working with him, but I never cried to him. (laughs)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-Stan_and_Roy-49)

Kirby had previously returned, in late 1956, to freelance on five issues [cover-dated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cover-date "Cover-date") December 1956 and February 1957,[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-53) but did not stay. Now, beginning with the cover and the seven-page story "I Discovered the Secret of the Flying Saucers" for _[Strange Worlds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strange\_Worlds\_(Atlas\_Comics) "Strange Worlds (Atlas Comics)")_ #1 (Dec. 1958), Kirby returned for a 12-year run that would soon help revolutionize comics. While career necessity led Kirby back to publisher Goodman, whom he had left acrimoniously in 1941, Kirby nonetheless helped elevate simple science fiction and giant-monster stories with what comics historian Charles Hatfield called "a vital jab in the ribs by [his] outlandish artistry.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-Hatfield-54):100 Soon his dynamic work began gracing countless covers and lead stories in the extant _[Strange Tales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strange\_Tales "Strange Tales")_ and the newly launched _[Amazing Adventures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazing\_Adventures "Amazing Adventures")_, _Strange Worlds_, _[Tales of Suspense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tales\_of\_Suspense "Tales of Suspense")_, _[Tales to Astonish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tales\_to\_Astonish "Tales to Astonish")_ and _[World of Fantasy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World\_of\_Fantasy "World of Fantasy")_. "Offsetting the formulaic nature of the stories was a dash of invigorating absurdity," wrote Hatfield. "The tales had Kirby's energy and, courtesy of Lee, confessional, first-person titles typical of sensation-mongering tabloids and comics, such as, 'I Created Sporr, the Thing That Could Not Die!'"[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-Hatfield-54):100–101

A Kirby science fiction/monster story, usually inked by [Christopher Rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Rule "Christopher Rule") initially, then by [Dick Ayers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Ayers "Dick Ayers") following Rule's retirement, would generally open each book. This was followed by one or two twist-ending thrillers or sci-fi tales drawn by [Don Heck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Heck "Don Heck"), [Paul Reinman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Reinman "Paul Reinman"), or [Joe Sinnott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Sinnott "Joe Sinnott"), all capped by an often-surreal, sometimes self-reflexive short by Lee and artist [Steve Ditko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Ditko "Steve Ditko"). Lee in 2009 described these "short, five-page filler strips that Steve and I did together", originally "placed in any of our comics that had a few extra pages to fill", as "odd fantasy tales that I'd dream up with [O. Henry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O._Henry "O. Henry")-type endings." Giving an early example of what would later be known as the "[Marvel Method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvel_Method "Marvel Method")" of writer-artist collaboration, Lee said, "All I had to do was give Steve a one-line description of the plot and he'd be off and running. He'd take those skeleton outlines I had given him and turn them into classic little works of art that ended up being far cooler than I had any right to expect."[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-55)

[Don Heck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Heck "Don Heck"), who worked as an Atlas staff artist from 1954 until the company's retrenchment in 1957 before returning the following year, recalled that the 1958 page rate "was around $20 per page to pencil and ink, I think [rival comic-book publisher] [DC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DC_Comics "DC Comics")'s average was $38. It didn't pick up until 1964-65, and even then it didn't go up all that much — a couple of bucks a page."[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-56)

Although for several months in 1949 and 1950 Timely's titles bore a circular logo labeled "Marvel Comic", the first modern comic books so labeled were the science fiction anthology _[Journey into Mystery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journey\_into\_Mystery "Journey into Mystery")_ #69 and the teen humor title _[Patsy Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patsy\_Walker\_(comic\_book) "Patsy Walker (comic book)")_ #95 (both June 1961), which each showed an "MC" box on its cover.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-57) However, collectors routinely refer to the company's comics from the April 1959 cover-dates onward (when they began featuring Jack Kirby artwork on his return to Goodman's company), as **pre-superhero Marvel**.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-58) Goodman would reuse the name Atlas for the [next comics company he founded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas/Seaboard_Comics "Atlas/Seaboard Comics"), in the 1970s.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-tcj114p97-59)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

US comic book publisher (1951–1957)

Atlas Comics[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/Atlas_Comics_logo.svg/250px-Atlas_Comics_logo.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Atlas_Comics_logo.svg)
Type[Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Division_(business) "Division (business)")
Industry[Publishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishing "Publishing")
Predecessor[Timely Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timely_Comics "Timely Comics")
Founded November 1951;74 years ago(1951-11)
Founder[Martin Goodman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Goodman_(publisher) "Martin Goodman (publisher)")
Defunct October 1957;68 years ago(1957-10)

Headquarters[Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan"), [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), U.S.
Key people[Martin Goodman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Goodman_(publisher) "Martin Goodman (publisher)")

**Atlas Comics** was the 1950s [comic-book](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comic_book "Comic book")[publishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishing "Publishing") label that evolved into [Marvel Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvel_Comics "Marvel Comics").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-1) Magazine and [paperback novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_market_paperback "Mass market paperback") publisher [Martin Goodman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Goodman_(publisher) "Martin Goodman (publisher)"), whose business strategy involved having a multitude of corporate entities, used Atlas as the umbrella name for his comic book division during this time. Atlas evolved out of Goodman's 1940s comic book division, [Timely Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timely_Comics "Timely Comics"), and was located on the 14th floor of the [Empire State Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_State_Building "Empire State Building"). This company is distinct from the 1970s comic-book company, also founded by Goodman, that is known as [Atlas/Seaboard Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas/Seaboard_Comics "Atlas/Seaboard Comics").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atlas_Comics_(1950s)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### After the Golden Age

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atlas_Comics_(1950s)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: After the Golden Age")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/6/64/YoungMen25.jpg/250px-YoungMen25.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:YoungMen25.jpg)

_Young Men_ #25 (Feb. 1954): Cover art by [Carl Burgos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Burgos "Carl Burgos").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-2) Note the Atlas globe in the top left corner.

Atlas Comics was the successor of [Timely Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timely_Comics "Timely Comics"), the company that [magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magazine "Magazine") and [paperback novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_market_paperback "Mass market paperback") publisher Martin Goodman founded in 1939, and which had reached the peak of its popularity during the war years with its star characters the [Human Torch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Torch_(Golden_Age) "Human Torch (Golden Age)"), the [Sub-Mariner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Namor_the_Sub-Mariner "Namor the Sub-Mariner") and [Captain America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_America "Captain America").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-3) The early to mid-1950s found comic books falling out of fashion due to competition from [television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television "Television") and other media.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-4)

Timely largely stopped producing superhero comics with the cancellation of _[Captain America Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain\_America\_Comics "Captain America Comics")_ at issue #75 ([cover-dated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cover-date "Cover-date") Feb. 1950), by which time the series had already been titled _[Captain America's Weird Tales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain\_America's\_Weird\_Tales "Captain America's Weird Tales")_ for two issues, with the finale featuring only anthological [suspense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suspense "Suspense") stories and no superheroes.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-5) The company's flagship title, _[Marvel Mystery Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvel\_Mystery\_Comics "Marvel Mystery Comics")_, starring the Human Torch, had already ended its run with #92 in June 1949,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-gcd-marvelmystery-6) as had _Sub-Mariner Comics_ with #32 the same month,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-gcd-GAsubmariner-7) and _The Human Torch_ with #35 in March 1949.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-gcd-GAHumanTorch-8) Timely made one more attempt at superheroes with the publication of _Marvel Boy_ #1-2 (Dec. 1950 - Feb. 1951),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-Brevoort-9):7 which was retitled _Astonishing_ with issue #3 (April 1951) and continued the _Marvel Boy_ feature through #6 (Oct. 1951).[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-11)

In the absence of superheroes, Goodman's comic book line expanded into a wide variety of genres, producing [horror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horror_comics "Horror comics"), [Westerns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_comics "Western comics"), [humor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humour "Humour"), [talking animal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talking_animals_in_fiction "Talking animals in fiction"), [drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drama "Drama"), [crime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crime_fiction "Crime fiction"), [war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_comics "War comics"), [jungle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jungle "Jungle"), [romance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romance_comics "Romance comics"), [espionage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spy_fiction "Spy fiction"), [medieval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages "Middle Ages") adventure, [Bible stories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bible_story "Bible story") and [sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sport "Sport") comics. As did other publishers, Atlas also offered comics about [models](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Model_(people) "Model (people)") and career women.

Goodman began using the logo of the Atlas News Company, the newsstand-distribution company he owned, on comics [cover-dated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cover-date "Cover-date") November 1951, even though another company, Kable News, continued to distribute his comics through the August 1952 issues, with its "K" logo and the logo of the independent distributors' union appearing alongside the Atlas globe.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-gcdatlasglobe-12) The Atlas logo united a line put out by the same publisher, staff and freelancers through 59 shell companies, from Animirth Comics to Zenith Publications.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-13) Soon afterwards, the company rejoined the [Association of Comics Magazine Publishers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Comics_Magazine_Publishers "Association of Comics Magazine Publishers") and begin using the "star" logo of ACMP on comics cover-dated between April 1952 and January 1955 on its titles, prior to the establishment of the [Comics Code Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comics_Code_Authority "Comics Code Authority").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-15)

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/8/83/Atlas_interior_logo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Atlas_interior_logo.jpg)

The logo treatment on a 1954 comic-book page, with "Atlas" as the comics brand

Atlas attempted to revive superheroes in _Young Men_ #24-28 (Dec. 1953 - June 1954) with the Human Torch (art by [Syd Shores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syd_Shores "Syd Shores") and [Dick Ayers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Ayers "Dick Ayers"), variously), the Sub-Mariner (drawn and most stories written by [Bill Everett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Everett "Bill Everett")) and [Captain America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_America "Captain America") (writer [Stan Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Lee "Stan Lee"), artist [John Romita Sr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Romita_Sr. "John Romita Sr.")). The short-lived revival also included restarts of _Sub-Mariner Comics_ (issues #33-42, April 1954 - Oct. 1955)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-16) and _Captain America_ (#76-78, May-Sept. 1954).[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-17) All three superheroes also appeared in the final two issues of _Men's Adventures_ (#27-28, May–July 1954).[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-18)

### Trend-following

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atlas_Comics_(1950s)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Trend-following")]

[![Image 7](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/6/6f/Astonishing30.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Astonishing30.jpg)

The pre-[Comics Code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comics_Code "Comics Code")_Astonishing_ #30 (Feb. 1954): Cover art by [Joe Maneely](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Maneely "Joe Maneely").

Goodman's publishing strategy for Atlas involved what he saw as the proven route of following popular trends in TV and [movies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movies "Movies") — [Westerns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_fiction "Western fiction") and war dramas prevailing for a time, [drive-in](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drive-in "Drive-in")[movie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movie "Movie") monsters another time — and even other comic books, particularly the [EC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertaining_Comics "Entertaining Comics")[horror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horror_(genre) "Horror (genre)") line.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-Daniels-20):67–68 As Marvel/Atlas editor-in-chief [Stan Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Lee "Stan Lee") told comic-book historian [Les Daniels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_Daniels "Les Daniels"), Goodman "would notice what was selling, and we'd put out a lot of books of that type." Commented Daniels, "The short-term results were lucrative; but while other publishers took the long view and kept their stables of heroes solid, Goodman let his slide."[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-Daniels-20):57

While Atlas had some horror titles, such as _[Marvel Tales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvel\_Tales\_(1949%E2%80%931957) "Marvel Tales (1949–1957)")_, as far back as 1949, the company increased its output dramatically in the wake of EC's success. Lee recalled, "[I]t was usually based on how the competition was doing. When we found that EC's horror books were doing well, for instance, we published a lot of horror books."[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-Daniels-20):67–68 Until the early 1960s, when Lee, [Jack Kirby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Kirby "Jack Kirby") and [Steve Ditko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Ditko "Steve Ditko") would help revolutionize comic books with the advent of the [Fantastic Four](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fantastic_Four "Fantastic Four") and [Spider-Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spider-Man "Spider-Man"), Atlas was content to flood newsstands with profitable, cheaply produced product — often, despite itself, beautifully rendered by talented if low-paid artists.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-21)

The Atlas "bullpen" had at least five staff writers (officially called editors) besides Lee: [Hank Chapman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hank_Chapman "Hank Chapman"), [Paul S. Newman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_S._Newman "Paul S. Newman"), [Don Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Rico "Don Rico"), [Carl Wessler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Wessler "Carl Wessler"), and, in the teen humor division, future _[Mad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mad\_(magazine) "Mad (magazine)")_ magazine cartoonist [Al Jaffee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jaffee "Al Jaffee"). [Daniel Keyes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Keyes "Daniel Keyes"), future author of _[Flowers for Algernon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flowers\_for\_Algernon "Flowers for Algernon")_, was an  editor beginning 1952.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-autobiop79-80-22) Other writers, generally freelance, included [Robert Bernstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Bernstein_(comics) "Robert Bernstein (comics)").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-bernsteingcd-23)

The artists — some freelance, some on staff — included such veterans as Human Torch creator [Carl Burgos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Burgos "Carl Burgos")[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-burgosgcd-24) and Sub-Mariner creator [Bill Everett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Everett "Bill Everett").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-gcd2-25) The next generation included the prolific and much-admired [Joe Maneely](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Maneely "Joe Maneely"), who before his death just prior to Marvel's 1960s breakthrough was the company's leading artist,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-26) providing many covers and doing work in all genres, most notably on Westerns and on the medieval adventure _[Black Knight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black\_Knight\_(Sir\_Percy) "Black Knight (Sir Percy)")_.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-gcd-joemaneely-27) Others included [Russ Heath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russ_Heath "Russ Heath"),[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-heathgcd-28)[Gene Colan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_Colan "Gene Colan"),[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-gcd-29) and the fledgling, highly individualistic [Steve Ditko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Ditko "Steve Ditko").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-ditkogcd-30)

Some of Atlas' prominent [Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_comics "Western comics") titles, many reprinted in the 1970s, were _[Ringo Kid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ringo\_Kid "Ringo Kid")_, with art by Maneely, [Fred Kida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Kida "Fred Kida") and John Severin; artist [Doug Wildey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doug_Wildey "Doug Wildey")'s _[The Outlaw Kid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outlaw\_Kid "Outlaw Kid")_; artist [Jack Keller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Keller_(comics) "Jack Keller (comics)")'s _[Kid Colt, Outlaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kid\_Colt,\_Outlaw "Kid Colt, Outlaw")_; the anthology _[Gunsmoke Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunsmoke\_Western "Gunsmoke Western")_, starring Kid Colt; and _[Black Rider](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black\_Rider\_(character) "Black Rider (character)")_, drawn by Maneely, [Syd Shores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syd_Shores "Syd Shores") and others.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-31)

### Humor and miscellanea

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atlas_Comics_(1950s)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Humor and miscellanea")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/f/f9/SgtBarneyBarker1.jpg/250px-SgtBarneyBarker1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SgtBarneyBarker1.jpg)

_Sergeant Barney Barker_ #1 (August. 1956), cover art by John Severin.

Atlas also published various children's and teen humor titles, including [Dan DeCarlo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_DeCarlo "Dan DeCarlo")'s _Homer, the Happy Ghost_ (a la _[Casper the Friendly Ghost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casper\_the\_Friendly\_Ghost "Casper the Friendly Ghost")_), _Homer Hooper_ (a la [Archie Andrews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Andrews "Archie Andrews")) and the [Joe Maneely](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Maneely "Joe Maneely")-drawn _Melvin the Monster_ (a la _[Dennis the Menace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennis\_the\_Menace\_(U.S.) "Dennis the Menace (U.S.)")_). _Sergeant Barney Barker_, drawn by John Severin, was Atlas' answer to _[Sgt. Bilko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Phil\_Silvers\_Show "The Phil Silvers Show")_.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-squa36-32)

One of the most long-running titles was _[Millie the Model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millie\_the\_Model "Millie the Model")_, which began as a Timely Comics humor series in 1945 and ran into the 1970s, lasting for 207 issues and launching spinoffs along the way. Created by writer-artist [Ruth Atkinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Atkinson "Ruth Atkinson"),[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-Manning-33):31 it later became the training ground for [cartoonist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartoonist "Cartoonist") DeCarlo — the future creator of _[Josie and the Pussycats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josie\_and\_the\_Pussycats\_(comic) "Josie and the Pussycats (comic)")_, _[Sabrina, the Teenage Witch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabrina,\_the\_Teenage\_Witch "Sabrina, the Teenage Witch")_ and other [Archie Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Comics "Archie Comics") characters, and the artist who established Archie Comics’ modern look.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-Manning-33):31[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-34) DeCarlo wrote and drew _Millie_ for 10 years.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-decarlogcd-35)

The high-school series _[Patsy Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patsy\_Walker\_(comic\_book) "Patsy Walker (comic book)")_, co-created by Atkinson and writer [Otto Binder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Binder "Otto Binder") in 1944,[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-36) featured art by [Al Hartley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Hartley "Al Hartley"), [Al Jaffee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jaffee "Al Jaffee"), [Morris Weiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Weiss "Morris Weiss") and others, and ran until 1967[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-37) It spun off three titles. Patsy herself would be integrated into [Marvel Universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvel_Universe "Marvel Universe") continuity years later as the [supernatural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supernatural "Supernatural") superheroine [Hellcat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellcat_(comics) "Hellcat (comics)").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-38)

Atlas' talking animal books featured [cartoonist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartoonist "Cartoonist")[Ed Winiarski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Winiarski "Ed Winiarski")'s trouble-prone _Buck Duck_, Maneely's mentally suspect _Dippy Duck_, and [Howie Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howie_Post "Howie Post")'s _The Monkey and the Bear_. Buck and the other animal characters briefly returned in the early 1970s when Marvel published the five-issue reprint title _Li'l Pals_ ("Fun-Filled Animal Antics!").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-lilpalsgcd-39)

Miscellaneous titles included the espionage series _[Yellow Claw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow\_Claw\_(character) "Yellow Claw (character)")_, with Maneely, Severin, and [Jack Kirby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Kirby "Jack Kirby") art; the [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Americans_in_the_United_States "Native Americans in the United States") hero _Red Warrior_, with art by [Tom Gill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Gill_(comics) "Tom Gill (comics)");[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-gillgcd-40) the [space opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_opera "Space opera")_Space Squadron_, written and drawn by future Marvel production executive [Sol Brodsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sol_Brodsky "Sol Brodsky");[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-brodskygcd-41) and _Sports Action_, initially featuring true-life stories about the likes of [George Gipp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Gipp "George Gipp") and [Jackie Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Robinson "Jackie Robinson"), and later fictional features of, as one cover headline put it, "Rugged Tales of Danger and Red-Hot Action!".[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-sportsactiongcd-42)

Staff artist [Stan Goldberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Goldberg "Stan Goldberg") recalled in 2005, "I was in the Bullpen with a lot of well-known artists who worked up there at that time. ... The guys ... who actually worked nine-to-five and put in a regular day, and not the freelance guys who'd come in a drop off their work ... were almost a hall of fame group of people. There was John Severin. [Bill Everett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Everett "Bill Everett"). [Carl Burgos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Burgos "Carl Burgos"). There was the all-time great Joe Maneely.... We all worked together, all the colorists and correction guys, the letterers and artists. ... We had a great time".[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-goldberg-43)

### Layoffs

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atlas_Comics_(1950s)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Layoffs")]

From 1952 to late 1956, Goodman distributed Atlas' comics to newsstands through his self-owned distributor, the Atlas News Company. He shut down Atlas News Company in 1956 and began newsstand distribution through [American News Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_News_Company "American News Company"),[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-gcdatlasglobe-12)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-Manning-33):66 the nation's largest distributor and a virtual [monopoly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monopoly "Monopoly"), which shortly afterward lost a [Justice Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Justice "United States Department of Justice")[lawsuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawsuit "Lawsuit") and discontinued its business. As comic-book historian [Gerard Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerard_Jones "Gerard Jones") explains, the company in 1956

> ...had been found guilty of restraint of trade and ordered to divest itself of the newsstands it owned. Its biggest client, [George Delacorte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Delacorte "George Delacorte"), announced he would seek a new distributor for his [Dell Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dell_Comics "Dell Comics") and paperbacks. The owners of American News estimated the effect that would have on their income. Then they looked at the value of the [New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey "New Jersey") real estate where their headquarters sat. They liquidated the company and sold the land. The company ... vanished without a trace in the [suburban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suburban "Suburban") growth of the 1950s.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-44)[_[page needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing\_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_]

The Atlas globe remained on the covers, however, until American News went out of business in June 1957.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-45) With no other options, Goodman turned to the distributor [Independent News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_News "Independent News"), owned by rival [National Periodical Publications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Periodical_Publications "National Periodical Publications"), the future [DC Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DC_Comics "DC Comics"), which agreed to distribute him on constrained terms that allowed only eight titles per month.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-Manning-33):66 The last comic to bear the Atlas globe on the cover was the comic _Dippy Duck_ #1,[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-46) and the first to bear the new "Ind." distributors' mark was _[Patsy Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patsy\_Walker\_(comic\_book) "Patsy Walker (comic book)")_ #73, both [cover-dated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cover-date "Cover-date") October 1957.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-47) The company was accordingly renamed to Goodman Comics after signing a distribution pact with [Independent News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_News "Independent News"), according to a 1960 trade article.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-48)

Stan Lee, in a 1988 interview, recalled that Goodman:

> ...had gone with the American News Company. I remember saying to him, 'Gee, why did you do that? I thought that we had a good distribution company.' His answer was like, 'Oh, Stan, you wouldn't understand. It has to do with finance.' I didn't really give a damn, and I went back to doing the comics. [Later,] we were left without a distributor and we couldn't go back to distributing our own books because the fact that Martin quit doing it and went with American News had gotten the wholesalers very angry ... and it would have been impossible for Martin to just say, 'Okay, we'll go back to where we were and distribute our books.' [We had been] turning out 40, 50, 60 books a month, maybe more, and [now] the only company we could get to distribute our books was our closest rival, National [DC] Comics. Suddenly we went ... to either eight or 12 books a month, which was all Independent News Distributors would accept from us.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-Stan_and_Roy-49)

During this retrenchment, according to a fabled industry story, Goodman discovered a closet-full of unused, but paid-for, art, leading him to have virtually the entire staff fired while he used up the inventory. In the interview noted above, Lee, one of the few able to give a firsthand account, told a seemingly self-contradictory version of the downsizing:

> It would never have happened just because he opened a closet door. But I think that I may have been in a little trouble when that happened. We had bought a lot of strips that I didn't think were really all that good, but I paid the artists and writers for them anyway, and I kinda hid them in the closet! And Martin found them and I think he wasn't too happy. If I wasn't satisfied with the work, I wasn't supposed to have paid, but I was never sure it was really the artist's or the writer's fault. But when the job was finished I didn't think that it was anything that I wanted to use. I felt that we could use it in inventory — put it out in other books. Martin, probably rightly so, was a little annoyed because it was his money I was spending.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-Stan_and_Roy-49)

In a 2003 interview, [Joe Sinnott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Sinnott "Joe Sinnott"), one of the company's top artists for more than 50 years, recalled Lee citing the inventory issue as a primary cause. "Stan called me and said, 'Joe, Martin Goodman told me to suspend operations because I have all this artwork in house and have to use it up before I can hire you again.' It turned out to be six months, in my case. He may have called back some of the other artists later, but that's what happened with me."[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-50)

### Pre-superhero Marvel

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atlas_Comics_(1950s)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Pre-superhero Marvel")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/92/StrangeWorlds1_Marvel.jpg/250px-StrangeWorlds1_Marvel.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:StrangeWorlds1_Marvel.jpg)

_[Strange Worlds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strange\_Worlds\_(Atlas\_Comics) "Strange Worlds (Atlas Comics)")_ #1 (Dec. 1958), the first Marvel/Atlas work by artist [Jack Kirby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Kirby "Jack Kirby") upon his permanent return to the company. Cover art by [penciler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penciler "Penciler") Kirby and [inker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inker "Inker")[Christopher Rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Rule "Christopher Rule").

Goodman's men's magazines and paperback books were still successful — the comics, except in the early Golden Age, were a relatively small part of the business — and Goodman considered shutting the division down. The details of his decision not to do so are murky. Artist [Jack Kirby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Kirby "Jack Kirby") — who had amicably split with creative partner [Joe Simon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Simon "Joe Simon") a few years earlier, and separately lost a lawsuit to a [DC Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DC_Comics "DC Comics") editor — was having difficulty finding work. He recalled that in late 1958,

> I came in [to the Marvel offices] and they were moving out the furniture, they were taking desks out — and I needed the work! ... Stan Lee is sitting on a chair crying. He didn't know what to do, he's sitting on a chair crying — he was still just out of his adolescence [Note: Lee, born Dec. 28, 1922, would actually have been about 36.] I told him to stop crying. I says, 'Go in to Martin and tell him to stop moving the furniture out, and I'll see that the books make money'.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-51)

The interviewer, _[The Comics Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Comics\_Journal "The Comics Journal")_ publisher [Gary Groth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Groth "Gary Groth"), later wrote of this interview in general, "Some of Kirby's more extreme statements ... should be taken with a grain of salt...."[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-52) Lee, specifically asked about the office-closing anecdote, said,

> I never remember being there when people were moving out the furniture. If they ever moved the furniture, they did it during the weekend when everybody was home. Jack tended toward hyperbole, just like the time he was quoted as saying that he came in and I was crying and I said, 'Please save the company!' I'm not a crier and I would never have said that. I was very happy that Jack was there and I loved working with him, but I never cried to him. (laughs)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-Stan_and_Roy-49)

Kirby had previously returned, in late 1956, to freelance on five issues [cover-dated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cover-date "Cover-date") December 1956 and February 1957,[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-53) but did not stay. Now, beginning with the cover and the seven-page story "I Discovered the Secret of the Flying Saucers" for _[Strange Worlds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strange\_Worlds\_(Atlas\_Comics) "Strange Worlds (Atlas Comics)")_ #1 (Dec. 1958), Kirby returned for a 12-year run that would soon help revolutionize comics. While career necessity led Kirby back to publisher Goodman, whom he had left acrimoniously in 1941, Kirby nonetheless helped elevate simple science fiction and giant-monster stories with what comics historian Charles Hatfield called "a vital jab in the ribs by [his] outlandish artistry.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-Hatfield-54):100 Soon his dynamic work began gracing countless covers and lead stories in the extant _[Strange Tales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strange\_Tales "Strange Tales")_ and the newly launched _[Amazing Adventures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazing\_Adventures "Amazing Adventures")_, _Strange Worlds_, _[Tales of Suspense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tales\_of\_Suspense "Tales of Suspense")_, _[Tales to Astonish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tales\_to\_Astonish "Tales to Astonish")_ and _[World of Fantasy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World\_of\_Fantasy "World of Fantasy")_. "Offsetting the formulaic nature of the stories was a dash of invigorating absurdity," wrote Hatfield. "The tales had Kirby's energy and, courtesy of Lee, confessional, first-person titles typical of sensation-mongering tabloids and comics, such as, 'I Created Sporr, the Thing That Could Not Die!'"[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-Hatfield-54):100–101

A Kirby science fiction/monster story, usually inked by [Christopher Rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Rule "Christopher Rule") initially, then by [Dick Ayers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Ayers "Dick Ayers") following Rule's retirement, would generally open each book. This was followed by one or two twist-ending thrillers or sci-fi tales drawn by [Don Heck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Heck "Don Heck"), [Paul Reinman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Reinman "Paul Reinman"), or [Joe Sinnott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Sinnott "Joe Sinnott"), all capped by an often-surreal, sometimes self-reflexive short by Lee and artist [Steve Ditko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Ditko "Steve Ditko"). Lee in 2009 described these "short, five-page filler strips that Steve and I did together", originally "placed in any of our comics that had a few extra pages to fill", as "odd fantasy tales that I'd dream up with [O. Henry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O._Henry "O. Henry")-type endings." Giving an early example of what would later be known as the "[Marvel Method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvel_Method "Marvel Method")" of writer-artist collaboration, Lee said, "All I had to do was give Steve a one-line description of the plot and he'd be off and running. He'd take those skeleton outlines I had given him and turn them into classic little works of art that ended up being far cooler than I had any right to expect."[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-55)

[Don Heck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Heck "Don Heck"), who worked as an Atlas staff artist from 1954 until the company's retrenchment in 1957 before returning the following year, recalled that the 1958 page rate "was around $20 per page to pencil and ink, I think [rival comic-book publisher] [DC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DC_Comics "DC Comics")'s average was $38. It didn't pick up until 1964-65, and even then it didn't go up all that much — a couple of bucks a page."[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-56)

Although for several months in 1949 and 1950 Timely's titles bore a circular logo labeled "Marvel Comic", the first modern comic books so labeled were the science fiction anthology _[Journey into Mystery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journey\_into\_Mystery "Journey into Mystery")_ #69 and the teen humor title _[Patsy Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patsy\_Walker\_(comic\_book) "Patsy Walker (comic book)")_ #95 (both June 1961), which each showed an "MC" box on its cover.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-57) However, collectors routinely refer to the company's comics from the April 1959 cover-dates onward (when they began featuring Jack Kirby artwork on his return to Goodman's company), as **pre-superhero Marvel**.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-58) Goodman would reuse the name Atlas for the [next comics company he founded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas/Seaboard_Comics "Atlas/Seaboard Comics"), in the 1970s.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_Comics_(1950s)#cite_note-tcj114p97-59)
